e.t: This word is a proper name, rendered “Abba” or “Avva.” It identifies a particular person rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs once, in 2 Chronicles 29:1. Because the verse text and surrounding context are not included here, the person’s role and the significance of the name in that passage cannot be stated from this word alone. Its basic meaning is therefore the personal name “Abba” or “Avva.”

Aber, also known as Aver, is a proper name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it identifies a particular person named in 1 Chronicles 4:18. The lexical information gives the name itself but does not provide an additional descriptive meaning. Because it occurs once in this corpus, its significance as a name must be understood from the surrounding passage and context.

This noun means “contention; agony”: intense struggle, distress, or painful inner conflict. It can describe a condition of severe anguish rather than a simple difficulty. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs three times, all in 2 Maccabees. The related sense of contention highlights struggle, while agony emphasizes the deep suffering that struggle may produce. Its precise force in any particular passage depends on the surrounding verse and context.

This verb means to “sense” or “perceive”—to recognize or take in something through understanding or awareness. It can describe grasping what is being said, noticing a reality, or receiving understanding, depending on the sentence around it. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs 11 times, with most occurrences in Old Testament books. Its precise force in any verse depends on the surrounding wording.

Aichioza, also given as Ekhioza, is a proper name rather than a common word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears once, in Joshua 15:61. The available lexical information preserves the name itself but does not identify whether it refers to a person, place, or another named entity. Its precise identification therefore depends on the surrounding passage and the name’s role in that passage.

gl: come to life again; return to life
d: come to life again; return to life

e.t: This Greek LXX verb means “come to life again” or “return to life.” It describes becoming alive once more, rather than simply continuing in an existing state of life. The word appears once in the Greek LXX corpus, in 2 Maccabees 7:9. Its precise force in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and passage, but its basic meaning is the return to life after death or lifelessness.

This Greek LXX noun means “relaxation” or “relief”—a release from strain, pressure, or troubling circumstances. It names a state in which tension is eased and rest or reprieve is experienced. The word occurs four times in the Greek LXX corpus, appearing twice in the Old Testament books represented here and twice in Sirach. Its precise force in any particular passage depends on the surrounding sentence, but its central idea remains an easing of hardship or distress.

This adjective describes someone who stands against another as an “opponent” or “competitor.” It presents a person as a rival in a contest or struggle, rather than simply naming a general difficulty or disagreement. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, in 4 Maccabees 3:5. The surrounding verse is needed to determine whether the emphasis falls on direct opposition, rivalry, or contest in that passage; the word itself identifies the opposing participant.

This noun describes an insatiable desire—a craving that is never satisfied—and can therefore mean greediness. It points to an excessive appetite for more rather than a moderate or necessary desire. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice, both times in Sirach 37:30–31. The word names the condition itself, not merely one particular act of taking or possessing. Its precise force in either verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central idea is a restless hunger that refuses to be content.

Ara is a proper name, referring to a person named Ara rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs 56 times. Its precise reference depends on the surrounding passage, since the name may identify different people in different genealogies or narratives. The word is also found in the Greek text of Genesis, Numbers, Job, Psalms, and other books.

Arnon is a proper name, referring to the place or feature called Arnon in the Greek Old Testament. It is not presented here as an ordinary descriptive word with a separate gloss; its meaning is its name, “Arnon.” The name occurs 32 times across 29 Old Testament verses in the Greek LXX, beginning in Exodus and continuing through Daniel. Its precise significance in any individual verse depends on that passage’s surrounding text.

Asar is a personal name in the Greek Septuagint, referring to an individual rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. The name is rendered “Asar” and appears three times in the Septuagint, all within Genesis 36. Because the available information identifies the name but does not provide its meaning or a verse’s surrounding narrative, its clearest sense is simply the proper name Asar. It occurs at Genesis 36:21, 36:27, and 36:30.

gl: mayor of the palace; chief of the court
d: mayor of the palace; chief of the court

e.t: This Greek LXX noun refers to the “mayor of the palace” or “chief of the court,” an official responsible for the royal household or court. It describes a position of authority within the king’s administration, rather than a general civic mayor in the modern sense. The word occurs once in the Greek Old Testament, at 2 Samuel 8:18. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning identifies a prominent palace official serving the king.

Aulōn, also rendered Avlon, is a proper name used for a specific place rather than a general idea or action. It appears twelve times in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical corpus, with occurrences from Deuteronomy through 3 Maccabees. Because no verse text or surrounding context is provided here, the name itself can be explained securely, while its precise geographic reference must be determined from each passage. It is not a common noun with a broader abstract meaning.

Babi, also rendered Vavi, is a personal name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. It identifies an individual in the Greek Old Testament’s rendering of Ezra. The name occurs four times, across three verses, all within Ezra. Because it is a proper name, its meaning is primarily identification: it points to the person named, while the surrounding passage supplies that person’s particular role or significance.

This word means “leech,” a noun naming that creature. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears once, in Proverbs 30:15. Its role as a noun identifies what is being referred to, while the word itself does not explain the larger point of the verse. Understanding that broader force requires the verse text and its surrounding context, which are not included here. The word’s basic meaning remains specific and concrete: “leech.”

This word means “treasury,” referring to a place or store where valuable things are kept. It is a noun, so it names such a store rather than describing an action. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Joshua 11:22. The precise force of the word in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and passage, but its basic meaning remains a treasury or valuable storehouse.

Gelmōn, also rendered Yelmon, is a proper name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. It appears twice in the Greek Old Testament wording of Numbers, in consecutive verses. Because it functions as a name, its meaning is primarily identification: it points to the particular person or place named in the passage, rather than expressing a general idea. The surrounding verse text is needed to identify precisely what or whom the name denotes.

Gob, also given as Gov, is a proper name rather than a word describing an object, action, or quality. In the Greek Old Testament text represented here, it occurs once, in 2 Samuel 21:19. The available lexical information identifies the name but does not provide a broader definition or a verse quotation. Its precise significance belongs to the surrounding passage, while its basic lexical function is simply to identify a named entity.

“Finger-sheath” refers to a covering or protective sheath for a finger. It is a noun naming a physical object, not an action or quality. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, in 4 Maccabees 8:13. The available lexical meaning identifies the object clearly, while the verse text is not available here to show how the writer uses it in that sentence. Thus, the safest ordinary reading is simply a sheath or covering associated with a finger.

Daleth is the name of a Hebrew letter. In the Greek LXX corpus, it appears once, in Psalms 118:25, functioning as a noun and identifying the letter rather than describing an action, person, or quality. Because no verse text or surrounding context is available here, its exact role in that occurrence cannot be explained further; its established lexical meaning is simply “daleth.”

This Greek LXX verb means “step through; go across.” It describes moving from one side or place to another, whether by crossing a boundary, passing through an area, or going onward. The basic idea is physical movement across or through something, while the surrounding sentence determines the exact English wording. It occurs 116 times in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical books, so it is a regularly used word for movement rather than a rare or specialized expression.

This verb means to lie in wait for someone continually. It describes persistent watchfulness with the purpose of catching or confronting a person, rather than a brief or accidental wait. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at 2 Samuel 3:30. Because the word appears only once and the verse text is not included here, its precise force in that passage must be understood from the surrounding context. The core idea remains sustained, deliberate waiting against someone.

e.h: To Let Down or Send In
e.t: This Greek LXX verb means “let down” or “to send in.” It describes causing something or someone to move downward or into a place, rather than merely being present there. The word appears once in the Greek Old Testament text represented here, at Exodus 23:33. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic action is a deliberate sending or lowering into a location.

Edene, also rendered Ethene, is a personal name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Ezra 10:30. Because the available information identifies the name but does not include the verse’s wording or surrounding context, its significance here is limited to identifying the person named. The spelling and rendering belong to the Greek LXX text and should not be treated as a separate Greek New Testament word.

This verb means to bear a hundredfold—to produce or yield an amount multiplied by one hundred. It describes unusually abundant increase rather than merely ordinary fruitfulness. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Genesis 26:12, so its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage. The word itself centers on the result: bearing or producing a hundred times as much. It is a specific expression of extraordinary increase.

This adjective means “intense,” describing something marked by great strength or force. It can characterize an experience, feeling, action, or condition that is not mild or weak. In the Greek LXX material, it appears twice, both times in 3 Maccabees. Its exact emphasis depends on the noun or situation it describes, but the central idea remains heightened strength or seriousness. The word itself does not specify whether that intensity is emotional, physical, or circumstantial; the surrounding sentence determines how its basic meaning is expressed.

This Greek LXX verb means “jump upon”: it describes the act of leaping onto something. As a verb, it expresses an action rather than naming a person, object, or quality. It occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus, in 1 Maccabees 9:48. The word’s precise force in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and passage, which are not included here; its basic lexical sense remains the movement of jumping upon something.

gl: of a year; one year old
d: of a year; one year old

e.t: This adjective means “of a year” or “one year old.” It describes something according to its age or its relation to a yearly period. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs 57 times, so its basic sense appears in descriptions involving age and year-based measures. The word itself supplies a time-related description rather than naming a person, object, or action. Its precise force in a particular verse depends on the noun or situation it describes.

This Greek LXX verb means “utterly dishonoured”: it describes someone being completely deprived of honor or treated with profound disgrace. As a verb, it expresses the action or state of bringing such dishonor upon someone. It occurs once in the Greek LXX, at Ezekiel 16:61, so its exact force there should be understood from that passage’s surrounding wording. The word’s central idea remains complete dishonor rather than a minor insult or ordinary loss of respect.

This Greek LXX noun means “putting on” or “laying on”—the act of placing something onto someone or something. It describes an action rather than the object being placed. The word appears five times in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical writings, across 2 Chronicles, Ezekiel, and 2 Maccabees. Its exact force in any verse depends on what is being placed and the surrounding sentence.

This verb means “interpret”: to explain or make the meaning of words understandable. In the Greek Old Testament, it describes the act of interpreting rather than the message itself. It occurs three times, in Ezra, Esther, and Job, showing that its basic sense is connected with making something understood. The precise force in any one passage depends on what is being interpreted and the surrounding context.

This Greek Old Testament noun means “eunuch,” naming a person designated by that term. It is used as a noun rather than expressing an action or quality. The word occurs 37 times in the LXX corpus, including Old Testament and deuterocanonical books, with especially frequent use in Esther and several occurrences in Kings and Genesis. Its precise significance in any particular passage depends on the surrounding verse and context.

Zebee is a proper name used to identify a particular person. It is not a common word describing an action, quality, or object, so its meaning is primarily the person whom the name identifies. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs 12 times across nine verses, appearing mainly in Judges and once in Psalms. The form is also rendered “Zevee,” showing that the name may be represented with a slightly different English spelling. Without the surrounding verse text, the name itself does not provide further information about the person’s character or role.

This Greek LXX noun refers to leadership or reign—the authority and responsibility involved in directing people or governing a realm. It can describe a ruling position, the exercise of authority, or the condition of being under a ruler. The word appears seven times in the Greek Old Testament and deuterocanonical writings represented here, including Genesis, Numbers, Sirach, and 4 Maccabees. Its precise force in a particular passage depends on the surrounding context.

This adjective means “half-dead.” It describes someone or something that is only partly alive, existing in a state between life and death. The word identifies a condition rather than an action or a character trait. In the Greek Old Testament (Septuagint) corpus represented here, it occurs once, in Wisdom 18:18. Its precise force in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and context, but its basic meaning remains a description of being half-dead.

This noun means “treasure”: valuable possessions or wealth kept, gathered, or held as a store. It can refer to material riches rather than to a person or action. In the Greek Old Testament and Deuterocanonical books, it occurs 91 times, showing that it is a normal word for stored riches and valuable goods across these writings. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage.

Iakim is a proper name used to identify a person in the Greek Old Testament. It is not presented here as a general word describing an action, quality, or object, so its meaning is simply the name Iakim. This name occurs four times in the Greek Old Testament, across Deuteronomy, 1 Samuel, and 1 Chronicles. The precise person identified depends on the surrounding verse and passage.

Iethet is a personal name, functioning as the designation of an individual rather than as a common word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament corpus represented here, it occurs once, at 1 Chronicles 1:51. The available information identifies the name itself but does not provide surrounding verse text, so its particular family or narrative role cannot be explained from the name alone.

This word means “supplication”: a humble, earnest appeal or prayer made to someone for help or favor. It is a noun, so it names the plea itself rather than the act of asking. In the Greek Old Testament writings represented here, it occurs seven times, including passages in Sirach, 2 Maccabees, and 3 Maccabees. Its central idea is a serious request offered with dependence and urgency, especially when the one making the appeal needs mercy, assistance, or a favorable response.

Joppe, also rendered Joppi, is a proper name for a place. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs nine times, appearing once in Jonah and repeatedly in 1 Maccabees, with one further occurrence in 2 Maccabees. The word itself identifies the place rather than describing an action, quality, or spiritual idea. Its significance in any particular passage must be understood from that passage’s surrounding text.

ἰχώρ is a noun meaning “ichor” or “etherial juice,” a distinctive fluid referred to by that name. The word is uncommon in this Greek LXX corpus, appearing three times: twice in Job and once in 4 Maccabees. Its basic meaning identifies the substance itself rather than an action, quality, or person. The precise force of the word in any one passage depends on the surrounding verse and its immediate context.

This verb means to “consecrate” or “dedicate”—to set a person or thing apart for a sacred purpose. It describes an act of giving something over to God or marking it as devoted to him. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs six times, including passages in Leviticus, 1 Chronicles, and 2 Maccabees. The surrounding context determines what is being dedicated and how that dedication is expressed.

This word means “means of stopping”: something that brings an action, movement, or process to an end. It is a noun, so it names the stopping measure or instrument rather than describing the act as a verb. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Sirach 36:12. Its precise force in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and context, but its central idea remains a means by which something is halted or brought to completion.

This Greek LXX verb means “burn down; burn up.” It describes setting something ablaze so that fire consumes or destroys it. As a verb, it expresses an action rather than a person, object, or quality. The word occurs seven times in the Greek LXX corpus, across both Old Testament and deuterocanonical writings. Its exact force in any individual passage depends on what is being burned and the surrounding sentence, but its central idea remains destructive burning by fire.

This Greek word means “go down” or “come down.” It is a verb describing movement from a higher place or position to a lower one. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs three times, including passages from Esther, Wisdom, and 2 Maccabees. Its basic sense remains physical or positional movement downward; the surrounding sentence determines exactly who moves and where. This is a Greek LXX word, distinct from Greek New Testament word entities.

This verb means “grind” or “pound,” describing the action of crushing or reducing something through repeated force. It is a physical action word rather than a name for the tool or material involved. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs three times, all within the Old Testament corpus. Its precise force in any particular passage depends on what is being acted upon and the surrounding sentence.

This Greek LXX noun means “cup,” referring to a vessel used to hold or measure liquid. In its eight occurrences in the Greek Old Testament, it appears especially in Leviticus 14 and Ezekiel 45, where cups are mentioned in connection with prescribed measures or offerings. The word therefore names an actual container, not an abstract idea. Its precise significance in any particular verse comes from the surrounding passage, but its ordinary meaning remains a cup or measured vessel.

This word means “authority” or “power”—the right, ability, or recognized strength to rule, command, or accomplish something. It is a noun describing power as something possessed or exercised, whether by a ruler or another powerful figure. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs five times, including a rendering as “power” in Isaiah 40:10. Its precise force in any particular passage depends on the surrounding sentence and subject.

Radiance means shining brightness or visible splendor. As a noun in the Greek Old Testament, it names the quality of giving off light or appearing brilliantly bright. The word occurs five times in this Greek Old Testament corpus, in Psalms, Isaiah, and Baruch. Its basic sense remains focused on brightness itself; the surrounding passage determines whether that radiance is being described as belonging to a person, a people, or something associated with divine glory.

Leukios, also rendered Lefkios, is a proper name identifying a person rather than describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament (Septuagint) corpus represented here, it occurs once, in 1 Maccabees 15:16. Because no verse text or surrounding context is provided, the name itself does not establish the person’s role or significance in that passage. Its meaning is therefore primarily identification.

This Greek LXX verb means “kill by hunger; starve.” It describes causing someone to die through lack of food, or reducing someone to extreme hunger. As a verb, it expresses an action rather than naming a person, object, or condition. It occurs once in the Greek Old Testament, in Proverbs 10:3. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning centers on death or severe deprivation caused by hunger.

Maatarōthorech is a proper name, rendered as “Maatarōthorech” or “Maatarothorekh.” It identifies a particular named entity rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. In the Greek Septuagint, this name occurs once, in Joshua 18:13. Because no verse text or surrounding context is available here, its specific significance in that passage cannot be stated safely; its established lexical function is simply that of a proper name preserved in the biblical place-name record.

Maria is a personal name, rendered as “Maria,” used to identify a person rather than describe an action, quality, or object. This word belongs to the Greek Old Testament (LXX), where it occurs 15 times in 13 verses. Its use is concentrated in Numbers, with additional occurrences in Exodus, 1 Chronicles, Deuteronomy, and Micah. As a proper name, its basic function is identification; the particular person it identifies must be determined from the surrounding verse and passage.

Μεγαλοπρεπῶς means “magnificently”: it describes an action done in a grand, impressive, or splendid manner. As an adverb, it tells how something is carried out rather than naming a person, object, or action itself. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs twice, once in 2 Maccabees 4:49 and once in 4 Maccabees 5:24. The surrounding verse text would determine what action is being described, but the word itself emphasizes greatness and splendor in the manner of doing it.

This word means the forehead, the front part of the head above the eyes. It is a noun naming a specific part of the human body. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs eight times across six verses, referring consistently to this bodily area. The word appears in passages from Exodus, 1 Samuel, 2 Chronicles, Isaiah, and Ezekiel. Its precise significance in any one passage comes from the surrounding verse and its subject, but its ordinary meaning remains straightforward: the forehead.

Moze is a proper name: it identifies a person rather than describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, the name occurs three times, appearing twice in Genesis and once in 1 Chronicles. Its recorded English rendering is “Moze,” so the name itself is the supported meaning. The surrounding verse text is not available here, and these references alone do not establish additional significance beyond identifying the person named.

This LXX verb means “grow insipid” or “make insipid”—to become dull or flavorless, or to cause something to lose its distinct quality. It can therefore describe either a change that happens or an action that produces that change. The word occurs five times in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, including four Old Testament occurrences and one in Sirach. Its precise force in any verse depends on the surrounding context.

This word refers to temple servants—people assigned to support the work and practical needs connected with the temple. It is a noun describing a recognized group rather than an individual title or personal name. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears 11 times in 10 verses, concentrated in Ezra and Nehemiah, where the returning community and temple arrangements are described. Its basic meaning remains focused on service carried out for the temple and its worshiping community.

Netōpha, also rendered Netofa, is a proper name. It identifies a named person or place in the Greek Old Testament, but the available wording does not specify which in each occurrence. This name appears twice in the Greek Old Testament corpus: once in Ezra 2:22 and once in Nehemiah 7:26. Its precise referent in either passage depends on the surrounding verse and passage context.

This noun refers to a newly ploughed field that had previously been left untilled. It describes ground that has been broken up and prepared for cultivation, emphasizing its changed condition from unused soil to land ready for planting. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Jeremiah 4:3. Its precise significance in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but the word itself points to freshly cultivated ground.

This adjective describes someone or something as having a sword in hand—that is, being sword-bearing or armed with a sword. It presents the sword as immediately held and ready, rather than merely owned or kept nearby. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, the word occurs once, in 4 Maccabees 16:20. Its precise force in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and passage, but its central meaning remains clear: a person characterized by carrying a sword in hand.

This Greek LXX noun means “suited to a slave; servile.” It describes a person or thing marked by the condition or manner of a slave, emphasizing servile character rather than freedom or high standing. The word occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus, in 3 Maccabees 2:28. Its precise force in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and context, but its basic meaning centers on something slave-like or appropriate to a slave.

This noun means “whole offering”: an offering understood as complete rather than only a portion. In the Greek Old Testament, it is used especially in passages concerning offerings and worship, with 190 occurrences across the LXX corpus. Its frequent appearance in Leviticus and Numbers reflects its close association with Israel’s sacrificial vocabulary. The word names the offering itself, while the surrounding passage determines the specific instructions or purpose connected with it.

This Greek LXX verb means “swear.” It describes the act of making an oath or solemnly affirming something. The word appears 169 times in the Greek Old Testament and deuterocanonical books represented in this corpus, so it is a recurring term for oath-taking rather than a rare expression. Its precise force in any individual verse depends on the surrounding statement and who is speaking.

This Greek LXX verb means to disparage or reproach someone—to speak of them in a demeaning, shaming, or accusing way. It describes words that belittle another person or bring blame against them. The related rendering “reproach” appears in several passages, including places where people are challenged or accused. In the Greek Old Testament and deuterocanonical writings represented here, the verb occurs 53 times, showing that it is a recurring way of describing verbal dishonor or blame. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage.

This Greek LXX word means “whatever.” It functions as a pronoun or adverb, pointing generally to an unspecified thing, person, matter, or circumstance rather than naming it directly. In ordinary use, it allows a statement to remain open-ended: the particular thing is not identified, or the exact choice is left unspecified. The word occurs four times in the Greek LXX corpus, appearing in Deuteronomy and the books of Maccabees. Its precise force in any one passage depends on the surrounding sentence and the matter being discussed.

This adverb means "visibly": in a way that can be seen clearly or is openly apparent. It describes how something is done or presented, rather than naming a person, object, or action by itself. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Esther 8:13. Its precise force in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and context, but its basic sense points to something evident to sight and not hidden from view.

This verb means to “exhibit side by side” or “reveal”—to place something before others so it can be seen or understood. It can describe making a matter plain by displaying it openly, rather than keeping it hidden. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it appears five times, including passages from Exodus, Ezekiel, Hosea, and Bel and the Dragon. The surrounding verse determines whether the emphasis falls on showing something visibly or making its significance clear.

παῦλα is a noun meaning “rest” or a “resting-point”—a pause or place where activity comes to an end. It describes relief from exertion or a stopping place, rather than an action performed by someone. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, in 2 Maccabees 4:6. The surrounding verse text is not available here, so the word’s exact force in that passage must be understood from its context. Its basic sense remains a point or period of rest.

This word means “persuasion”—an appeal or reasoning intended to convince someone. As a noun, it refers to the condition or result of being persuaded rather than the act of speaking itself. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at 2 Kings 18:19. Its precise force in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and passage, but its basic sense remains the gaining of agreement or confidence through convincing words or reasons.

This word means “leaf,” referring to a thin, flat piece such as a leaf-like plate or sheet. It is a noun used in the Greek Old Testament, especially in descriptions of priestly garments and the construction of sacred furnishings. The word occurs seven times in seven verses in the Greek Old Testament, from Exodus through 1 Kings. Its precise sense in any individual verse comes from the object being described, but its central idea remains a leaf or similarly thin flat piece.

This adjective describes someone or something as prolific, especially as giving birth to many children. It expresses abundant childbearing rather than merely productivity in a general sense. In the Greek Old Testament, this word occurs once, at Psalm 143:13, and is rendered “prolific.” Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding context, but its basic meaning points to fertility and many births.

This verb means “saw”: it names the action of cutting with a saw. In the Greek Old Testament (the LXX), it appears once, in Amos 1:3, so this entry represents a single occurrence rather than a widely repeated biblical usage. The word functions as a verb, describing what someone does with a saw. Its basic meaning is concrete and practical; the surrounding verse determines any further significance.

This verb means “worship”: to direct reverence and devotion toward someone or something regarded as worthy of honor. In the Greek Old Testament, it is used for an act of worship rather than merely describing a person or object. The word occurs 190 times in the LXX corpus, showing that worship is a recurring scriptural action involving both the worshiper and the one receiving worship. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage.

This verb means to call someone in alongside others or to invite them. It describes an action of bringing a person into a setting, gathering, or conversation rather than merely speaking to someone from a distance. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, in 2 Maccabees 12:31. Its precise force in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and passage, but its central idea is an invitation or summons to come near and join those already present.

This Greek LXX word means “frequent,” describing something that happens often or at short intervals. It can function as an adjective or adverb, so it may characterize a thing or describe repeated action. Within the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs seven times, including six occurrences in deuterocanonical books and one in Esther. The precise nuance in any passage depends on the surrounding context.

Ramessai, also rendered Rhamesse, is a proper name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. It identifies a person named in the Greek Old Testament. This name occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus, at 1 Chronicles 7:10. Without the surrounding verse text, Scripture does not provide enough here to explain more about the person’s identity or role; the securely supported meaning is the personal name itself.

Rasia is a proper name, referring to a person rather than describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament (LXX), it occurs once, at 1 Chronicles 7:39. The available rendering gives the name as “Rasia,” while the related gloss also records “Rhasia,” preserving the name’s identity rather than translating it into an ordinary descriptive word. Its precise role in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but the word itself functions as a personal name.

This word means “pomegranate-orchard,” referring to a cultivated place where pomegranate trees grow. It is a noun used in the Greek Old Testament to name such a grove or orchard. The word occurs six times in the LXX, across Numbers, 1 Kings, Zechariah, and Song of Songs. Its repeated use in descriptions of land, buildings, and gardens shows that it identifies a recognizable agricultural place rather than a person, action, or abstract idea.

Samari is a proper name—the identifying name “Samari,” rather than a general descriptive word. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears only once, at 1 Chronicles 4:37. The word itself supplies the name, while the surrounding verse is needed to determine whom or what Samari names. It should therefore be understood as a preserved name, not expanded into an assumed meaning or description beyond the name itself.

This word means “prudence”—careful, sensible judgment in deciding how to act. As a noun, it refers to the quality of thinking wisely rather than acting rashly. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Ezra 8:18. The word’s concise sense points to practical wisdom and sound judgment, while the surrounding verse is needed to determine exactly how that quality functions in that passage.

Sellemi or Sellimi is a proper name in the Greek LXX of the Old Testament. It does not describe an action, quality, or object; rather, it serves as the personal name by which an individual is identified. This name occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus, at Numbers 26:49. No separate everyday meaning is attached to the name here. The person it identifies must be understood from the surrounding passage.

This noun means “ashes”: the powdery remains left after something has been burned. It names a physical substance used in several Old Testament and deuterocanonical passages translated from the Greek Old Testament. The word occurs 35 times in this Greek Old Testament corpus, including references in Genesis, Numbers, Esther, Job, and Psalms. Its precise significance in any particular passage depends on the surrounding verse and scene.

This Greek LXX noun means “support”: something that holds up, strengthens, or provides stability. It can describe practical help or a sustaining foundation, depending on the sentence in which it appears. The word occurs 16 times in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical books represented here, so it is not limited to one kind of setting. Its basic idea remains consistent: support that enables something or someone to stand, continue, or remain secure.

This noun refers to a closed place or a refuge—a location that provides enclosure, shelter, or protection. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek Jewish Scriptures, it occurs 10 times, describing the idea of being shut in or having a secure place of safety. Its meaning can apply to a physical enclosure or a place where someone is protected from danger, depending on the surrounding passage.

This word means “fig,” the fruit that grows on a fig tree. It is a noun used for an individual fig or for figs as a group, depending on the sentence. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs seven times, all within seven verses, especially in Jeremiah, and also in Isaiah and Nehemiah. The word can therefore refer simply to the fruit itself, while the surrounding passage determines whether the figs are being described as present, absent, good, or ruined. Its precise force in any one verse depends on that passage’s wording.

This Greek LXX verb means “meet with.” It describes the action of encountering or coming together with another person or party. As a verb, it expresses something someone does rather than naming a person, place, or object. The word appears 59 times in this Greek Old Testament and Deuterocanonical corpus, showing that it is a recurring way to describe an encounter. Its precise force in a particular verse depends on the surrounding context.

The word occurs twice in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented in this corpus, once in Job and once in 2 Maccabees. Its precise force in either passage depends on the surrounding verse context, which is not included here.

This Greek LXX noun means “victim”: a person or creature subjected to harm, slaughter, or sacrificial action. It identifies the one acted against rather than the one performing the action. The word occurs five times in the Greek Old Testament represented here, appearing once in Leviticus, three times in Ezekiel, and once in Amos. Its central meaning remains consistent across these occurrences: someone or something regarded as a victim. The exact force in any particular verse depends on that verse’s surrounding context.

“Sōphach; Sofakh” is a proper name, referring to a particular person rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. In the Greek Old Testament, this name occurs twice, both times in 1 Chronicles 19—at verses 16 and 18. The word’s basic meaning is therefore its identity as a personal name; understanding the person’s role requires the surrounding verse and passage, which are not included here.

Taberemman, also rendered Taveremman, is a proper name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. The name occurs once in the Greek Old Testament, at 1 Kings 15:18. The available wording preserves the name but does not identify from the name alone whether it refers to a person, place, or other named entity. Its precise referent must therefore be understood from the surrounding passage.

This noun refers to an officer, with the related sense of a knight or military official. It describes a person holding a position of authority in an army or royal force, rather than an ordinary soldier. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs nine times, appearing in Exodus and 2 Kings. Its exact force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage, but the central idea is an appointed military officer or commander.

This noun means “delicacy” or “daintiness,” describing a delicate condition or quality rather than an action or person. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Deuteronomy 28:56. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding wording, but the central idea remains a state marked by delicacy or daintiness. The English rendering “delicacy” expresses this same basic meaning.

This Greek LXX noun means “loosening” or “weakening,” describing a loss of firmness, strength, or stability. It appears once in the Greek Old Testament, in Nahum 2:11. The word’s basic sense points to something becoming less tightly held together or less strong. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but the central idea remains a reduction of strength or firmness.

This verb means to murder—to kill a person unlawfully and deliberately. It describes the act of taking human life, especially in passages dealing with justice, guilt, refuge, and punishment. The word occurs 48 times in this Greek biblical corpus, showing a consistent sense rather than a broad range of meanings. Its use in commands and legal discussions presents murder as a serious offense requiring judgment. The surrounding verse determines the specific circumstances, but the word itself centers on the wrongful killing of another person.

This verb means “lower”: to bring something down from a higher position or level. It describes an action rather than a person, object, or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs four times, in passages from Exodus, Isaiah, and Jeremiah. Its exact force may refer to lowering a physical object or bringing something down in another setting, so the surrounding verse determines the immediate application. The central idea remains a downward movement or change of position.

Chezrath, also rendered Khezrath, is a proper name rather than a general word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Septuagint, it occurs once, at 1 Kings 15:20. The available lexical information identifies it as a named entity, but does not provide a broader definition or enough verse text to explain its specific role in that passage. Its precise significance there must therefore be understood from the surrounding biblical context.

This noun means “dancing.” It names the activity of dancing rather than describing a person or functioning as a verb. In the Greek Septuagint corpus, it occurs 19 times across 19 verses, in both the Old Testament and deuterocanonical books. Its appearances range from Exodus through Song of Songs, showing that the word is used as a straightforward noun for dancing in different biblical settings. The surrounding passage determines the particular scene, but the word’s basic meaning remains dancing.

This word means “well.” It is an adverb, so it describes how an action is carried out or how something is regarded: it is done or understood well. Its meaning is broad but simple, expressing a positive manner or quality rather than naming a person, object, or event. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs once, at Wisdom 8:1; the surrounding verse is needed to explain its particular force there.

This verb means to have contractions, describing the physical process associated with childbirth. It presents contractions as an action or experience rather than naming a person or object. In the Greek Septuagint, it occurs 19 times, showing that the term is used across several Old Testament and deuterocanonical writings. Its exact force in any passage depends on the surrounding sentence, but its central meaning remains the experience of contractions.
